summary:
Brook Riggio addresses the 2025 challenge of deploying zero-ops, resilient, agent-powered apps on serverless infrastructure. The landscape is overwhelming, with options across client apps, agent frameworks, orchestration layers, and serverless platforms. LLMs cannot reliably guide assembly of these stacks due to lack of training data.

Riggio's recommended stack: Next.js (streaming, server actions, file-based routing, deep Vercel integration), OpenAI's Agents SDK (native tool calling, one-shot and multi-agent calls, built-in tracing and eval hooks, model interchangeability), Inngest (event-driven, automatic retry, step-level observability, one-click Vercel integration), and Vercel (preview deployments, edge network, automatic CDNs, integrated databases).

The architecture flows from user to Next.js, which checks a database for cached results, then triggers an Inngest event. Inngest orchestrates Python serverless functions running OpenAI Agents SDK agents. The Inngest workflow is structured with each step defined at the top, each calling a function below for clear orchestration. Step one calls the research agent, step two formats the newsletter with a formatting agent, and step three saves results to Vercel blob storage. Code outside step.run may execute multiple times as Inngest determines which step to run, but code inside step.run runs reliably in sequence with results passed between steps.

Local development requires three terminals: Python agents, Next.js, and Inngest dev server. Deployment uses the Vercel CLI, which auto-detects the project structure—including the API agents folder deployed as a Python 3.12 function—without a vercel.json config file. Only two environment variables are needed: an OpenAI API key and a Vercel blob storage token. The complete demo repo is open-sourced on GitHub, with an invitation for contributions and community examples.

sections.title: Introduction and the 2025 Challenge
sections.summary: Riggio introduces himself and frames the central question of 2025: how to deploy zero-ops, resilient, agent-powered apps. He surveys the overwhelming landscape of client apps, agent frameworks, orchestration layers, and serverless platforms, estimating millions of combinations and noting that LLMs cannot reliably guide assembly of these stacks.

sections.title: The Recommended Stack
sections.summary: Riggio details his preferred stack: Next.js for streaming and server actions, OpenAI's Agents SDK for native tool calling and tracing, Inngest for event-driven orchestration with automatic retry and step-level observability, and Vercel for preview deployments, edge network, and integrated databases. He emphasizes these tools work together reliably.

sections.title: Architecture and Demo App
sections.summary: Riggio outlines the architecture: user connects to Next.js, which checks a database and triggers Inngest events; Inngest orchestrates Python serverless functions running OpenAI Agents SDK agents; results are cached and returned to the frontend. He demonstrates a newsletter generator app taking comma-separated topics, showing the Inngest dev server breaking tasks into steps and the app polling the database for results.

sections.title: Code Walkthrough
sections.summary: Riggio walks through the project structure: Inngest endpoint served from the app, newsletter API endpoints that invoke Python agents, a top-level API directory where Vercel auto-serves each file as an independent function, and an Inngest workflow folder. The AI agents are powered by FastAPI with research and formatting endpoints. No vercel.json config file is needed.

sections.title: Inngest Workflow and Deployment
sections.summary: Riggio details the Inngest workflow structure: steps defined at the top each call functions defined below, keeping high-level orchestration clear. Step one calls the research agent, step two formats the newsletter, step three saves to blob storage. He warns that code outside step.run may execute multiple times, but step.run code runs reliably in sequence with results passed between steps. He then demonstrates deployment via Vercel CLI, showing build logs with Python 3.12 function auto-detection, pulling environment variables (OpenAI API key and Vercel blob storage token) from production, and invites the audience to fork the open-source repo and contribute examples.
